rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch claim and the proof gap in separate containers, then tells the founder which angles to pitch now and which to hold. Its best line, "Replit will tell you it builds working apps — it won't tell you how often they actually work," is an editor-ready tension; B has the same instinct, but it gets loose when it says "you pay by the job — not by the seat," which is not what the facts say. B is strong material, but it buys too much theater with unsupported pegs.
gaps_in_A: "one English sentence" over-specifies the launch. The update says a plain-English description, not a single sentence.
"You pay per build" invents the metering unit. The facts only say usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, and A later admits the unit is unknown.
"AI compute gets passed to the user" is plausible, but it is still an inference until Replit discloses rates or metering logic.
The education angle depends on agent use in classrooms, and A knows it: "only timely if Replit can point to actual classroom use of the agent." Without that, it is a smart maybe, not a pitch.
gaps_in_B: "you pay by the job — not by the seat" overstates the pricing fact. The update says usage-based on top of subscriptions, not a replacement for subscription or seat pricing.
"a tool that writes the code for students" turns Replit's education usage into student access to this agent. That may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
"CS teachers are already arguing about" and "this school year" add a topical peg without evidence from the update. Useful instinct, sloppy sourcing.
"The people building apps on Replit now are the ones who never learned to build them" asserts actual user behavior. The facts give positioning for non-engineers, not adoption or a named user.
